questions.stem: A wholesaler sends a Class II recall notice identifying one lot of a blood-pressure medication. The pharmacy has bottles from the affected lot and from an unaffected lot, and several patients previously received the affected lot. What is the best immediate pharmacy response?

choices.text: Stop dispensing every strength and lot of the drug until the manufacturer ends the recall.
Segregate the affected lot, preserve lot traceability, and follow the recall notice for inventory and patient follow-up.
Continue dispensing the affected lot until each patient confirms whether the medication caused symptoms.
Tell every patient taking the drug to stop therapy immediately, regardless of the recalled lot or notice.
Return only unopened affected bottles and leave opened affected bottles available for completion of existing prescriptions.

explanation.core_reasoning: The legal and operational decision is lot-specific. The pharmacy removes the identified lot from availability, preserves traceability, and follows the recall notice rather than expanding or narrowing the recall on its own.

choice_analysis.A: The recall is lot-specific; unaffected stock is not automatically removed from use unless the notice directs that broader action.
choice_analysis.B: This matches the lot-specific recall response: remove affected stock from availability, preserve traceability, and follow the notice's instructions.
choice_analysis.C: A recalled lot should not remain available for dispensing while the pharmacy waits for symptom reports.
choice_analysis.D: A recall does not automatically mean every patient using every lot should stop therapy; the pharmacy follows the recall's risk and patient instructions.
choice_analysis.E: Affected stock is segregated from dispensing based on the recall, not kept available because a bottle has already been opened.

related_facts: Recall notices may identify specific lots, strengths, or packages.
Patient instructions depend on the recall notice and risk, not merely on the word 'recall'.
explanation.mpje_trap: A recall is not an automatic order to stop every patient's therapy or destroy every lot of the product.

reasoning_steps: Identify the exact recalled lot and affected inventory
Separate inventory action from patient clinical instructions

questions.stem: A pharmacy refrigerator is found at 68°F after an overnight equipment failure. Several unopened insulin glargine cartons were stored there, and the pharmacy cannot yet determine how long the temperature was outside the labeled storage range. What should the pharmacist do with those cartons before dispensing?

choices.text: Dispense them normally because unopened prescription stock cannot be adulterated until it reaches a patient.
Relabel each carton with the observed temperature and dispense if the patient accepts the excursion.
Segregate the cartons from saleable stock and resolve product integrity under the labeling/manufacturer information before dispensing.
Return the cartons to refrigeration for one hour; restoring temperature automatically restores legal saleability.
Convert the cartons to patient-return inventory and use the ordinary returned-drug resale rule.

explanation.core_reasoning: The pharmacy must not dispense stock whose storage excursion leaves strength, purity, or quality unresolved. Segregation and product-specific assessment come before any decision to return the stock to saleable inventory.

choice_analysis.A: Pharmacy-owned stock can become unsuitable or adulterated before dispensing when storage conditions compromise quality.
choice_analysis.B: Patient consent does not establish the product's strength, quality, or storage integrity.
choice_analysis.C: A material unresolved storage excursion calls for segregation and quality assessment before the product is made available.
choice_analysis.D: Returning stock to the refrigerator does not prove that an excursion caused no quality problem.
choice_analysis.E: This is pharmacy-owned stock affected by storage conditions, not medication returned from a patient.

related_facts: Drug integrity can be affected by storage conditions while stock remains pharmacy-owned.
A patient-return rule and a pharmacy storage-excursion rule address different facts.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not confuse a storage excursion with the separate rule governing medications returned by a patient.

reasoning_steps: Identify the excursion as a product-integrity issue
Prevent dispensing until integrity is resolved

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a valid oxycodone Schedule II prescription for 30 tablets but has only 12 tablets in stock. The patient wants the full prescribed quantity; the pharmacy dispenses 12 solely because it cannot supply the rest. Four days later the remaining stock arrives. What is the controlling federal consequence?

choices.text: The balance may be dispensed within 30 days because every Schedule II partial fill uses the patient-requested 30-day pathway.
The pharmacy may treat the remaining 18 tablets as a refill because the original total quantity was not dispensed.
The remaining 18 tablets may be transferred to another pharmacy once the original pharmacy receives stock.
The ordinary 72-hour shortage-remainder period has passed, so further quantity generally requires prescriber notification and a new prescription.
The original pharmacy may dispense the balance at any time before the Massachusetts 30-day Schedule II validity period ends.

explanation.core_reasoning: The reason for the partial fill determines the legal pathway. A pharmacy-stock shortage invokes the federal 72-hour remainder framework, not the patient-requested 30-day framework.

choice_analysis.A: The initial partial fill was caused by pharmacy inability, not the patient's election to receive a lesser quantity.
choice_analysis.B: Schedule II prescriptions are not refilled; the shortage remainder is governed by the specific partial-fill rule.
choice_analysis.C: A shortage remainder is not transformed into a transferable refill.
choice_analysis.D: For a partial fill caused by inability to supply the full quantity, the federal shortage pathway generally requires the remainder within 72 hours.
choice_analysis.E: The general prescription-validity period does not displace the shorter federal shortage-remainder rule.

related_facts: Patient-requested and pharmacy-inability partial fills have different predicates.
A Schedule II remainder is not a refill.
explanation.mpje_trap: Ask why the first partial fill occurred before choosing a deadline.

reasoning_steps: Classify why the first partial fill occurred
Apply the shortage-specific remainder rule
Reject the refill analogy

questions.stem: A father asks a Massachusetts community pharmacy to obtain a prescription-labeled naloxone product through the pharmacy's authorized naloxone prescription/standing-order pathway because his adult daughter recently survived an opioid overdose. The daughter is not present. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: The pharmacy must refuse because naloxone may be supplied only to the person at risk.
The father must first be diagnosed with opioid use disorder before he can receive naloxone.
The request must be processed as an emergency Schedule II opioid prescription.
A lawful Massachusetts naloxone pathway can include a person positioned to assist someone at risk of overdose.
Community pharmacies may provide naloxone only when an emergency department transfers the patient’s prescription.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts opioid-antagonist access is intentionally broader than direct-to-patient dispensing. A family member positioned to respond to an overdose can fall within the lawful third-party access framework.

choice_analysis.A: The law does not require the naloxone recipient to be the person who is personally at risk.
choice_analysis.B: The assisting person need not have opioid use disorder to qualify as a third-party recipient.
choice_analysis.C: Naloxone access is not governed by treating naloxone as a Schedule II opioid.
choice_analysis.D: This matches the third-party assistance purpose of the Massachusetts naloxone framework.
choice_analysis.E: The statute contemplates pharmacy access and is not limited to emergency-department transfers.

related_facts: Prescription naloxone and FDA-labeled OTC naloxone are separate products under current Massachusetts DCP guidance.
Massachusetts prescription naloxone access can place rescue medication with a third party positioned to assist.
explanation.mpje_trap: The person receiving the naloxone does not have to be the person expected to receive naloxone during an overdose.

reasoning_steps: Identify the requester as a third party positioned to assist
Apply the Massachusetts opioid-antagonist access rule

questions.stem: A patient at risk of opioid overdose asks a Massachusetts pharmacy for a prescription-labeled naloxone product. The patient has no patient-specific naloxone prescription, but the pharmacy participates in an authorized statewide standing-order prescription pathway. What is the key legal point?

choices.text: A patient-specific office prescription is the only lawful pharmacy pathway for naloxone.
The standing-order pathway may authorize dispensing when its requirements are met, so absence of a separate patient-specific prescription is not automatically disqualifying.
A standing order can be used only for Schedule II opioids and never for an opioid antagonist.
The pharmacist must convert naloxone into a controlled-substance Schedule before the standing order can be used.
Standing-order authority applies only when the requester is a family member rather than the person at risk.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts pharmacy naloxone access can operate through an authorized standing order. The pharmacist should determine whether that pathway applies rather than assuming that only a conventional patient-specific prescription can support dispensing.

choice_analysis.A: Massachusetts provides a broader pharmacy access mechanism than a patient-specific prescription alone.
choice_analysis.B: A valid standing order can supply the prescribing authority for an otherwise eligible naloxone dispensing encounter.
choice_analysis.C: The standing-order mechanism is not limited to dispensing the opioids that naloxone is intended to reverse.
choice_analysis.D: Naloxone’s access does not require assigning it a federal controlled-substance schedule.
choice_analysis.E: The pathway can serve the person at risk as well as other qualifying recipients.

related_facts: The statewide standing order can serve as prescription authority for prescription naloxone when its requirements are met.
FDA-labeled OTC naloxone is a separate product and does not become Schedule VI merely because prescription naloxone also exists.
explanation.mpje_trap: Ask what authority supports the dispensing, not whether a traditional prescription sheet exists.

reasoning_steps: Identify the absence of a patient-specific prescription
Identify the pharmacy’s standing-order authority
Determine whether the standing order can support the naloxone dispensing

questions.stem: A clonazepam Schedule IV prescription is written for 90 tablets. The patient asks to receive 30 tablets today and the rest in later partial dispensings. Which statements describe the federal partial-fill framework? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Each partial dispensing is recorded in the same manner as a refill.
The first 30-tablet partial dispensing automatically cancels all authority to dispense the remaining quantity.
The total quantity dispensed through all partial fills may not exceed the quantity prescribed.
The partial-dispensing sequence must remain within the applicable six-month federal prescription period.
The patient may extend the partial-dispensing period indefinitely by requesting smaller quantities each month.

explanation.core_reasoning: Schedule III-V partial filling is permitted, but it is bounded by recordkeeping, cumulative-quantity, and timing rules. The patient can choose staged dispensing without creating unlimited additional quantity or time.

choice_analysis.A: Federal law directs the pharmacy to record each Schedule III-V partial filling in the same manner as a refilling.
choice_analysis.B: Schedule III-V prescriptions may be partially filled when the regulatory conditions are met.
choice_analysis.C: The aggregate of all partial dispensings is capped by the original prescribed quantity.
choice_analysis.D: Federal Schedule III-V partial filling may not continue beyond six months after issue.
choice_analysis.E: Patient requests do not extend the federal time limit.

related_facts: Partial fills are recorded like refills.
Total partial quantities cannot exceed the prescription and must remain within six months.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not equate permission to partial-fill with permission to enlarge the quantity or extend the prescription clock.

reasoning_steps: Classify the drug as Schedule IV
Apply the partial-fill record and quantity conditions
Apply the six-month outer time limit

questions.stem: A manufacturer representative leaves several sealed prescription-drug sample packs marked 'sample - not for resale' at a community pharmacy after a clinic declines them. The pharmacy manager proposes entering them into normal inventory and dispensing them on paid prescriptions. What is the best legal response?

choices.text: Do not place the samples into ordinary saleable pharmacy inventory; samples follow the authorized sample-distribution pathway.
The pharmacy may sell the samples after removing the 'not for resale' statement from the outer package.
The pharmacy may bill only cash patients for the samples because insurance billing is the sole federal restriction.
The pharmacy may dispense the samples if a pharmacist records a zero acquisition cost in the perpetual inventory.
The pharmacy may convert the samples to stock after holding them for 30 days without a manufacturer recall.

explanation.core_reasoning: The key fact is that the products are prescription drug samples, not ordinary wholesaler-acquired pharmacy stock. A pharmacy cannot cure that distribution restriction by changing billing, inventory value, or packaging.

choice_analysis.A: Prescription drug samples are not ordinary saleable inventory and must remain within the authorized sample-distribution framework.
choice_analysis.B: Relabeling does not convert a prescription drug sample into lawful saleable inventory.
choice_analysis.C: The restriction concerns the sample-distribution pathway, not merely the method of payment.
choice_analysis.D: Inventory accounting does not authorize redistribution of prescription drug samples as normal stock.
choice_analysis.E: No waiting period changes the sample's legal distribution status into ordinary saleable inventory.

related_facts: Prescription drug sample controls concern distribution channels.
A 'not for resale' sample does not become ordinary stock because it is unopened.
explanation.mpje_trap: The issue is the product's lawful distribution channel, not whether the pharmacy can account for it financially.

reasoning_steps: Identify the products as prescription drug samples
Separate sample distribution from ordinary pharmacy acquisition and dispensing

questions.stem: A patient presents a valid oxycodone Schedule II prescription for 20 tablets and tells the pharmacist, before any dispensing, that she wants only 8 tablets because she is concerned about keeping extra opioid tablets at home. The pharmacy has all 20 tablets in stock. Which action is supported by Massachusetts law?

choices.text: Refuse the request because Schedule II prescriptions must be dispensed only in the exact quantity written.
Dispense all 20 tablets and advise the patient to discard the unwanted tablets at home.
Change the prescription quantity to 8 only after obtaining a replacement prescription from the prescriber.
Dispense the requested lesser quantity and document the partial dispensing in the patient record.
Treat the request as a pharmacy-stock shortage and use the federal 72-hour remainder rule.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts gives the patient an option to receive less than the prescribed Schedule II quantity. The pharmacist should identify the patient's election and document the lesser dispensing rather than forcing the full amount or misclassifying it as a stock shortage.

choice_analysis.A: Massachusetts specifically allows a patient to request a lesser Schedule II quantity.
choice_analysis.B: The law provides a lesser-quantity option; unnecessary dispensing is not required.
choice_analysis.C: The patient's statutory lesser-quantity election can be honored without converting it into a new prescriber-written quantity.
choice_analysis.D: This applies the Massachusetts patient lesser-quantity option and its documentation requirement.
choice_analysis.E: The pharmacy can supply the full quantity; the predicate is the patient's election, not pharmacy inability.

related_facts: The lesser-quantity option is patient driven.
A pharmacy shortage invokes a different partial-fill pathway.
explanation.mpje_trap: The quantity is lower because the patient chose less, not because the pharmacy lacked stock.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the patient is choosing a lesser quantity
Document the lesser Schedule II dispensing

questions.stem: During closing procedures, a Massachusetts pharmacy discovers that its controlled-substance storage cabinet no longer locks. The inventory reconciles and no theft or loss is known. A technician suggests leaving the controlled stock there overnight because the alarm system covers the building. What is the best response?

choices.text: Leave the stock in place because a theft report is required only after an actual loss is proved.
Move or otherwise secure the controlled stock under compliant restricted-access conditions before closing and address the failed security control.
Convert all controlled stock to will-call prescriptions so the cabinet no longer contains pharmacy inventory.
Wait until the next biennial inventory to determine whether the broken lock caused a reportable discrepancy.
File DEA Form 106 immediately even though no theft or significant loss has been discovered.

explanation.core_reasoning: Security and loss reporting are separate decisions. Here the pharmacy has discovered a failed security control but no loss; it should secure the controlled substances and restrict access rather than waiting for a discrepancy or inventing a theft report.

choice_analysis.A: The absence of a known loss does not eliminate the pharmacy's independent duty to maintain secure controlled-substance storage and access.
choice_analysis.B: The operative problem is a known physical-security failure; the pharmacy should restore secure storage/access before leaving the stock unattended.
choice_analysis.C: Changing inventory labels does not cure the underlying physical-security failure.
choice_analysis.D: Biennial inventory does not substitute for ongoing controlled-substance security.
choice_analysis.E: A security defect requires correction, but the stated facts do not establish a theft or significant loss for a Form 106 event.

related_facts: Controlled-substance security is continuous, not limited to inventory dates.
A security defect and a confirmed significant loss trigger different duties.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not wait for a theft to occur before correcting a known controlled-substance security failure.

reasoning_steps: Separate a security defect from a theft/loss event
Restore compliant restricted access before leaving the inventory unattended

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist legally changes her name and moves to a new home address. She updates payroll and her employer's personnel system the same week but makes no update to her Board licensure record. What additional compliance step is required?

choices.text: No Board action is needed because employer records are the controlling professional-license record.
Wait until the next pharmacist license renewal and report both changes only on the renewal application.
Report the specified name and contact-information changes to the Board within the applicable 14-day period.
Report only the legal name change; a residential-address change is never part of Board contact information.
File a pharmacy facility amendment because an individual pharmacist's home-address change alters the pharmacy license.

explanation.core_reasoning: Professional-license reporting is independent of employer HR records. When a specified personal-status or contact change occurs, the licensee must update the Board within the rule's reporting period.

choice_analysis.A: Employer records do not replace the licensee's separate duty to report specified changes to the Board.
choice_analysis.B: The change-reporting rule uses a shorter reporting period rather than waiting for renewal.
choice_analysis.C: This applies the Board's individual-licensee change-reporting rule.
choice_analysis.D: Specified contact-information changes are part of the reporting framework.
choice_analysis.E: The facts concern the individual licensee's record, not a facility relocation or license amendment.

related_facts: The trigger is a change in the licensee's reportable information.
Employer notification and Board notification serve different records.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not substitute an employer's internal update for the licensee's direct Board-reporting duty.

reasoning_steps: Identify the changes as individual-licensee information
Apply the Board's 14-day reporting requirement

questions.stem: A pharmacist lawfully dispensed a three-day emergency oral Schedule II prescription after speaking directly with the prescriber. Eight days later, the pharmacy still has not received the required follow-up prescription despite documented requests to the prescriber. What federal step now becomes important for the pharmacist?

choices.text: Convert the emergency dispensing into a Schedule III refill so the existing record can remain open.
Delete the emergency prescription record because the prescriber failed to complete the follow-up.
Wait until 30 days after the oral authorization because the prescriber still has the full Schedule II validity period.
Reverse the original dispensing claim and treat the medication as an undocumented sample.
Notify DEA of the prescriber's failure to deliver the required emergency follow-up prescription.

explanation.core_reasoning: This question starts after the emergency dispensing has already occurred. Once the prescriber misses the required follow-up deadline, the pharmacist's issue is no longer whether the emergency was valid but what federal post-dispensing notification duty applies.

choice_analysis.A: A Schedule II emergency dispensing cannot be converted into a Schedule III refill.
choice_analysis.B: The dispensing record must be retained; deletion would not resolve the missed follow-up duty.
choice_analysis.C: The emergency follow-up rule uses its own seven-day deadline.
choice_analysis.D: Billing reversal does not change the legal fact that an emergency Schedule II dispensing occurred.
choice_analysis.E: After the seven-day follow-up failure, federal law places a DEA-notification duty on the pharmacist.

related_facts: The emergency oral Schedule II pathway has a seven-day follow-up requirement.
The pharmacist has a separate duty when the prescriber fails to deliver that follow-up.
explanation.mpje_trap: Memorizing 'seven days' is incomplete; know what the pharmacist must do when day seven passes without the follow-up.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the dispensing used the emergency oral Schedule II pathway
Determine that the seven-day follow-up deadline passed
Apply the pharmacist's DEA-notification duty

questions.stem: The pharmacist who normally signs a pharmacy's CSOS Schedule II orders is on vacation. Her DEA-issued CSOS certificate is installed on the ordering workstation, and another pharmacist knows the software password but has not been issued that certificate. May the second pharmacist use the installed certificate to sign today's oxycodone order?

choices.text: No. The CSOS certificate may be used to sign orders only by the individual subscriber to whom DEA issued it.
Yes, because any pharmacist working under the same pharmacy DEA registration may use any installed certificate.
Yes, if the second pharmacist prints the electronic order after signing and stores it with paper Forms 222.
Yes, but only when the order contains fewer than twenty Schedule II line items.
No, because CSOS can never be used for Schedule II orders when paper Form 222 is available.

explanation.core_reasoning: CSOS uses an individual digital identity. The pharmacy may have multiple authorized subscribers, but one employee cannot simply use another subscriber's DEA-issued certificate because the certificate is installed on a shared machine.

choice_analysis.A: CSOS signing authority is personal to the named subscriber; access to the workstation or password does not transfer that authority.
choice_analysis.B: The certificate belongs to the individual subscriber, not to every pharmacist associated with the registrant.
choice_analysis.C: Printing a record does not cure unauthorized use of another person's digital certificate.
choice_analysis.D: Line-item limits do not authorize certificate sharing.
choice_analysis.E: CSOS is an authorized electronic alternative to paper Form 222; the defect here is who would sign with the certificate.

related_facts: CSOS certificates are issued to individuals.
A shared workstation does not make a personal signing certificate a shared credential.
explanation.mpje_trap: Separate the pharmacy's DEA registration from the individual subscriber's authority to apply the digital signature.

reasoning_steps: Identify whose CSOS certificate would sign the order
Determine whether that individual is the DEA-issued subscriber

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a prescription for mifepristone 200 mg for medical termination of pregnancy through 10 weeks. The pharmacy is not currently certified in the Mifepristone REMS Program. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Retail pharmacies are categorically prohibited from dispensing mifepristone, even if they become REMS-certified.
The pharmacy must satisfy the current Mifepristone REMS pharmacy-certification requirements before dispensing under this pathway.
The prescription must come from a prescriber who satisfies the current Mifepristone REMS prescriber-certification requirement.
Massachusetts Schedule VI status does not erase the separate federal product-specific REMS conditions.
The pharmacy can substitute ordinary Schedule VI transfer documentation for REMS certification because mifepristone is not federally controlled.

explanation.core_reasoning: The pharmacist must apply both the ordinary Massachusetts prescription framework and the product-specific federal REMS. Retail dispensing is possible, but only through the current certified-pharmacy/certified-prescriber pathway.

choice_analysis.A: Current FDA rules allow retail pharmacy dispensing when the pharmacy satisfies the REMS certification requirements.
choice_analysis.B: Pharmacy certification is a current REMS condition for pharmacy dispensing of the drug for this indication.
choice_analysis.C: The current REMS requires a certified prescriber for this use.
choice_analysis.D: State Schedule VI classification and federal REMS requirements operate as different legal layers.
choice_analysis.E: Ordinary state prescription mechanics do not replace the product-specific federal REMS gate.

related_facts: FDA permits certified retail pharmacies to dispense mifepristone under the REMS.
A REMS restriction is distinct from controlled-substance scheduling.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not infer 'not federally controlled' to mean 'no federal dispensing restriction'.

reasoning_steps: Identify the product and REMS-governed indication
Check pharmacy certification
Check prescriber certification
Keep REMS separate from Schedule VI status

questions.stem: A visitor from another country asks to buy one small package containing 60 mg total pseudoephedrine. The visitor has only a foreign passport and no identification document accepted by the federal CMEA retail-ID rule. The sale otherwise stays within all quantity limits. Which federal point is most relevant?

choices.text: A foreign passport always satisfies the CMEA retail-ID requirement for any pseudoephedrine quantity.
The sale is prohibited because every pseudoephedrine purchase, including a 60 mg single package, requires the ordinary logbook and ID process.
A single sales package containing no more than 60 mg may use the narrow exception from the ordinary purchaser-ID and logbook transaction requirement.
The pharmacist may waive identification for any purchase under the 3.6 gram daily limit.
The visitor may buy any amount if another adult with acceptable identification signs the logbook instead.

explanation.core_reasoning: This is not a gram-limit question. The decisive fact is that the request is for one sales package containing no more than 60 mg, which DEA identifies as a narrow exception to the ordinary individual ID/logbook transaction requirement.

choice_analysis.A: DEA guidance states that a foreign passport does not itself satisfy the ordinary CMEA identification rule described for these purchases.
choice_analysis.B: Federal law provides a narrow single-package exception at no more than 60 mg.
choice_analysis.C: DEA identifies this narrow exception for one sales package containing no more than 60 mg of pseudoephedrine.
choice_analysis.D: The daily quantity limit and the separate ID/logbook gate are different requirements.
choice_analysis.E: The purchaser's own identity and transaction must satisfy the applicable rule; another person cannot simply sign in place of the purchaser.

related_facts: CMEA quantity limits and ID/logbook rules are separate gates.
The 60 mg rule is a narrow single-package exception, not a general low-dose waiver.
explanation.mpje_trap: Passing the daily quantity limit does not answer the ID question; look for the single-package 60 mg exception.

reasoning_steps: Separate quantity compliance from purchaser-ID compliance
Recognize the single-package 60 mg exception

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain opens a new Massachusetts location and stocks pseudoephedrine behind the counter. Employees completed the chain's CMEA training, but the new physical location has not yet completed the DEA self-certification process. May the location begin covered retail pseudoephedrine sales because another store in the chain is already certified?

choices.text: Yes, because one current chain-level self-certification automatically covers every future physical store.
No. The new location must satisfy its own applicable CMEA self-certification requirement before covered retail sales begin.
Yes, if all sales remain below 3.6 grams per purchaser per day.
No, because employee training and DEA self-certification are mutually exclusive alternatives and the chain chose training.
Yes, but only for electronic-logbook sales during the first 30 days after opening.

explanation.core_reasoning: CMEA compliance includes store-level seller obligations in addition to transaction-level limits. The new location cannot borrow another location's certification simply because ownership and training materials are shared.

choice_analysis.A: DEA's current self-certification process treats separate physical retail locations as separately certified locations.
choice_analysis.B: The physical location needs its own applicable self-certification; another store's certification does not authorize it.
choice_analysis.C: Quantity compliance does not replace the seller's certification requirement.
choice_analysis.D: Training and seller self-certification are related compliance duties, not alternatives.
choice_analysis.E: No startup grace period based on electronic logbook use substitutes for required seller compliance.

related_facts: DEA's online process identifies separate physical locations for self-certification.
Employee training does not replace the location's applicable certification.
explanation.mpje_trap: Distinguish chain ownership from the physical-location unit used for CMEA seller certification.

reasoning_steps: Identify the seller as a new physical location
Check training and self-certification as separate prerequisites

questions.stem: A patient presents a valid clozapine prescription in August 2026. A pharmacist trained under the former Clozapine REMS tells a colleague that the pharmacy cannot dispense until the patient is enrolled in the REMS and an ANC result is entered into that program. What is the current federal position?

choices.text: The former REMS enrollment and ANC-verification gate remains mandatory for every clozapine dispensing.
The pharmacy may ignore any clinically significant blood-count information because removal of the REMS ended all clozapine monitoring concerns.
The pharmacy must enroll only the prescriber, while pharmacy and patient enrollment are no longer required.
FDA removed the Clozapine REMS, so REMS enrollment and REMS ANC verification are no longer federal dispensing prerequisites, although clinical monitoring remains relevant.
Clozapine became an over-the-counter drug when the REMS was removed.

explanation.core_reasoning: FDA removed the Clozapine REMS effective in 2025. The pharmacist should not continue imposing the former program as a legal dispensing gate, while still addressing clinically meaningful monitoring under current labeling and professional practice.

choice_analysis.A: FDA removed the Clozapine REMS and no longer requires those program steps as dispensing prerequisites.
choice_analysis.B: Removal of the REMS did not eliminate the drug's clinical neutropenia risk or labeling-based monitoring recommendations.
choice_analysis.C: FDA removed the REMS program itself rather than retaining a prescriber-only enrollment gate.
choice_analysis.D: This reflects FDA's current post-REMS framework.
choice_analysis.E: Removal of a REMS does not change clozapine from prescription to OTC status.

related_facts: REMS removal does not convert a prescription drug to OTC status.
Clinical monitoring and a REMS enrollment gate are different concepts.
explanation.mpje_trap: A historical safety program may no longer be a current legal prerequisite even though the underlying clinical risk remains.

reasoning_steps: Determine the current REMS status as of the dispensing date
Separate REMS eligibility from ongoing clinical monitoring

questions.stem: During final verification of a Massachusetts alprazolam prescription, the pharmacist notices that the dispensing label has the patient, drug, directions, pharmacy, prescriber, and prescription number but omits some other information required by M.G.L. c. 94C §21. Which items should be corrected before dispensing? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Add the date the prescription is being filled.
Add the patient's health-plan member identification number.
Add the filling pharmacist's initials.
Add the wholesaler invoice number for the bottle used to fill the prescription.
Because tablets are being dispensed, add the number of tablets in the container.

explanation.core_reasoning: The container label has its own statutory checklist. Final verification should compare the actual label against the Massachusetts dispensing-label requirements rather than importing insurance or wholesaler fields.

choice_analysis.A: Massachusetts requires the fill date on the controlled-substance container label.
choice_analysis.B: The statute does not make the insurance member ID a required controlled-substance container-label element.
choice_analysis.C: The filling pharmacist's initials are among the statutory label elements.
choice_analysis.D: The wholesaler invoice number is not a required patient container-label element under this statute.
choice_analysis.E: For tablets or capsules, the statute requires the number in the container on the label.

related_facts: The label rule is distinct from the information required on the prescription itself.
Tablet or capsule count is expressly addressed by the statute.
explanation.mpje_trap: A valid prescription can still produce a noncompliant dispensed container if required label information is missing.

reasoning_steps: Identify this as a dispensing-label review
Match missing fields to M.G.L. c. 94C §21

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses buprenorphine-naloxone, Schedule III, to a patient specifically for treatment of opioid use disorder. A technician asks whether the state Schedule II/III consumer-education pamphlet must accompany this dispensing. Which conclusion best applies?

choices.text: Yes, because every Schedule III dispensing requires the pamphlet with no indication-based exceptions.
No. The statute excepts Schedule II or III drugs prescribed for substance use disorder or opioid-dependence treatment.
No, because buprenorphine-naloxone is Massachusetts Schedule VI rather than Schedule III.
Yes, unless the prescriber writes 'pamphlet not required' on the prescription.
No, because the pamphlet requirement applies only to Schedule II stimulants.

explanation.core_reasoning: The pharmacist first identifies that the drug falls within Schedule III, then checks the statutory exceptions. Because the prescription is for OUD treatment, the specific exception controls the pamphlet decision.

choice_analysis.A: The statute contains express exceptions, including treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.
choice_analysis.B: This dispensing fits the statutory exception for treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.
choice_analysis.C: Buprenorphine-naloxone is federally and Massachusetts Schedule III; the exception turns on the treatment use, not Schedule VI status.
choice_analysis.D: The statutory exceptions do not depend on a prescriber writing that notation.
choice_analysis.E: The statute reaches narcotics or controlled substances in Schedule II or III, subject to its exceptions.

related_facts: The rule covers Schedule II and III but contains setting/indication exceptions.
Buprenorphine-naloxone remains Schedule III even when used for OUD.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not stop after classifying the schedule; the indication can change the pamphlet requirement.

reasoning_steps: Classify the medication as Schedule III
Identify the stated OUD treatment indication
Apply the statutory exception

questions.stem: During a Board-readiness walkthrough, a Massachusetts community pharmacy that dispenses Schedule II through V prescriptions has no prescription lock boxes for sale and no notice about them near the pharmacy counter. The manager says patients can buy lock boxes online instead. What is the best compliance assessment?

choices.text: The pharmacy complies because online retail availability satisfies the pharmacy's obligation.
Only pharmacies that dispense more than a threshold number of opioids must carry lock boxes.
The pharmacy needs only a verbal counseling script; physical availability and signage are optional.
The store should make prescription lock boxes available for sale and display the required notice on or near the pharmacy counter.
The requirement applies only to institutional pharmacies, not community pharmacies.

explanation.core_reasoning: This is a facility-operation requirement, not a counseling preference. A covered store must satisfy both the on-site availability and notice components rather than redirecting patients to outside sellers.

choice_analysis.A: The statute places the availability and notice duties on each covered store location.
choice_analysis.B: The statutory trigger is the covered pharmacy's registration to dispense Schedule II-V prescription drugs, not an opioid-volume threshold.
choice_analysis.C: The statute specifically addresses lock boxes for sale and a posted notice.
choice_analysis.D: This is the store-level duty created by M.G.L. c. 94C §21B.
choice_analysis.E: The statute targets covered pharmacies and excludes specified institutional settings rather than limiting the rule to them.

related_facts: The duty is tied to each covered store location.
Patient lock boxes are different from the pharmacy's own controlled-substance storage.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not confuse a patient-facing lock-box sales requirement with internal pharmacy security controls.

reasoning_steps: Identify the pharmacy as a covered Schedule II-V dispenser
Check both product availability and counter notice

questions.stem: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, an insured patient's adjudicated cost-sharing amount for a generic prescription is $18. The pharmacy's current retail cash price for the same prescription is $11. The prescription is otherwise ready for sale. What amount does the Massachusetts point-of-sale rule require the pharmacy to charge?

choices.text: $18, because an insurer-adjudicated cost share always overrides the pharmacy retail price.
$14.50, because the pharmacy must split the difference between the two prices.
$11, because the pharmacy charges the lesser of the applicable cost-sharing amount and the pharmacy retail price.
$18 unless the patient affirmatively asks to be treated as an uninsured cash customer before claim adjudication.
$0, because a difference between retail price and cost sharing voids the patient's payment obligation.

explanation.core_reasoning: The pharmacist or point-of-sale process compares the two defined amounts. Because the pharmacy retail price is lower than the applicable cost share, the pharmacy charges the retail price.

choice_analysis.A: Massachusetts requires comparison of the applicable cost share and pharmacy retail price rather than automatically collecting the higher cost share.
choice_analysis.B: The statute does not create an averaging formula.
choice_analysis.C: The retail price is lower on these facts, so it is the amount the statute selects.
choice_analysis.D: The point-of-sale rule itself requires the lesser amount; it is not conditioned on a special opt-out request in the stated facts.
choice_analysis.E: The law chooses the lower amount; it does not automatically eliminate payment.

related_facts: The comparison is made at the point of sale.
The rule protects against collecting a cost share that exceeds the pharmacy retail price.
explanation.mpje_trap: An insurance claim result is not automatically the amount the pharmacy may collect when state law requires the lower comparison.

reasoning_steps: Identify the two amounts the statute compares
Select the lesser amount

questions.stem: A customer asks a Massachusetts drugstore's front-end clerk to sell a package of hypodermic syringes intended for injection of a controlled substance. The store contains a licensed pharmacy, but the clerk is not a pharmacist and wants to complete the sale independently at the front register. What is the best legal response?

choices.text: Route the transaction through an authorized seller under M.G.L. c. 94C §27, such as the pharmacist, rather than having the clerk independently make the sale.
The clerk may complete the sale because any employee of a premises containing a pharmacy is automatically treated as a pharmacist for §27.
The sale is prohibited at every retail pharmacy because syringes may be sold only by hospitals.
The clerk may sell the syringes only after entering the transaction in the DEA pseudoephedrine logbook.
The clerk may complete the sale if the customer presents a Schedule II prescription.

explanation.core_reasoning: The question is who may conduct the sale. Massachusetts §27 identifies authorized categories of sellers, including a pharmacist; the existence of a pharmacy inside the store does not automatically give unrelated front-end staff that statutory role.

choice_analysis.A: The statute limits these sales to listed categories of authorized sellers, including a pharmacist.
choice_analysis.B: The statute identifies authorized seller categories; mere employment by a store containing a pharmacy does not make the clerk a pharmacist.
choice_analysis.C: The statute expressly includes pharmacists among authorized sellers.
choice_analysis.D: Pseudoephedrine CMEA logbook requirements do not govern a syringe sale.
choice_analysis.E: A Schedule II prescription does not convert an unauthorized seller into a statutory seller under §27.

related_facts: The statute regulates the seller category.
Syringe-sale authority is separate from pseudoephedrine and prescription-fill rules.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not substitute the store's pharmacy license for the individual seller category named in the statute.

reasoning_steps: Identify the product and intended use described by §27
Determine whether the proposed seller is within an authorized category

questions.stem: A known Massachusetts prescriber telephones a new warfarin prescription to the pharmacist. Warfarin is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug. Which actions correctly apply to this oral prescription? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Because Schedule VI is excluded from §20(c)'s later follow-up-prescription requirement, the pharmacist does not need to create an oral-prescription record.
The pharmacist should immediately reduce the oral prescription to writing with the information required by Massachusetts law.
The pharmacist must demand a replacement electronic prescription within two days because §20(c) applies identically to Schedule VI.
The Schedule VI exception from the later follow-up document does not eliminate the pharmacist's ordinary authenticity and validity responsibilities.
The pharmacist must convert the prescription to Schedule V before an oral transmission can be accepted.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts separates the immediate oral-prescription record from the later follow-up-document rule. Schedule VI is excepted from the latter, not from the pharmacist's contemporaneous documentation and validity duties.

choice_analysis.A: The Schedule VI exception concerns the later follow-up document; the pharmacist still immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing.
choice_analysis.B: Section 20(a) requires contemporaneous reduction of the oral controlled-substance prescription to writing.
choice_analysis.C: Section 20(c) expressly states that its later electronic/written follow-up requirements do not apply to Schedule VI.
choice_analysis.D: Schedule VI remains a prescription controlled substance under Massachusetts law; the follow-up exception is not a blanket validity waiver.
choice_analysis.E: An oral Schedule VI prescription does not become Schedule V; classification is not changed by transmission method.

related_facts: M.G.L. c. 94C §20(a) applies to oral controlled-substance prescriptions.
Section 20(c) expressly excludes Schedule VI from its later follow-up prescription requirement.
explanation.mpje_trap: A statutory exception can be narrow: identify exactly which step it removes and which duties remain.

reasoning_steps: Classify warfarin as Massachusetts Schedule VI
Separate immediate oral documentation from later follow-up documentation
Apply the narrow Schedule VI exception

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy licensed for sterile compounding prepares a patient-specific sterile compounded infusion for outpatient use. The ordinary prescription label is complete, but the final container does not identify the preparation as compounded and does not display the pharmacy's required pharmacist-contact telephone number. What should happen before the product leaves the pharmacy?

choices.text: Dispense it because ordinary prescription-label elements make all compounded-product labeling requirements optional.
Remove the ordinary prescription label and use only the word 'sterile' on the container.
Correct the container to identify the sterile compounded preparation and include the required pharmacist-contact information before outpatient dispensing.
Dispense it unchanged if the patient has previously received another compounded medication from the pharmacy.
Treat the missing information only as a continuing-education issue for the compounding pharmacist.

explanation.core_reasoning: The pharmacy must verify the compounded product itself, not just the prescription. Massachusetts adds a compounded-preparation designation and, for covered sterile/complex nonsterile compounding pharmacies, required pharmacist contact information for outpatient products.

choice_analysis.A: Massachusetts imposes additional compounded-preparation labeling and, for covered pharmacies, pharmacist-contact requirements.
choice_analysis.B: The additional compounded-product information supplements rather than replaces ordinary applicable labeling duties.
choice_analysis.C: The facts describe a covered outpatient sterile compounded preparation missing the additional statutory label/contact elements.
choice_analysis.D: Prior patient experience does not waive the product-specific label and communication requirements.
choice_analysis.E: The defect is on the dispensed product and communication label, not merely the pharmacist's CE record.

related_facts: Compounded-drug labeling is distinct from compounding CE.
The institutional inpatient exception does not fit an outpatient dispensing.
explanation.mpje_trap: A complete ordinary prescription label can still be incomplete for a compounded preparation.

reasoning_steps: Identify the preparation as outpatient sterile compounded product
Apply the additional compounded label and contact requirements

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is considering a nonprescription retail sale of a medicinal preparation that has already been confirmed to qualify for the controlled-substance exception described in M.G.L. c. 94C §4. Which §5 controls still apply to the sale? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The purchaser must identify themself to the pharmacist's satisfaction.
The pharmacist must keep the required purchaser/product sale record.
Because the product qualifies for an exception, any amount may be sold in a single transaction without a time-based limit.
The pharmacist must observe the four-ounce-per-person limit during a 48-hour period.
The sale must be processed as a Schedule II emergency oral prescription.

explanation.core_reasoning: An excepted preparation is not an unrestricted OTC item. The special retail pathway remains conditioned on identification, quantity/time limits, good-faith medicinal sale, and recordkeeping.

choice_analysis.A: Section 5 conditions the retail exception on purchaser identification satisfactory to the pharmacist.
choice_analysis.B: The statute requires an accurate record including purchaser and preparation information.
choice_analysis.C: The exception is conditional; §5 imposes a four-ounce per person/48-hour limit.
choice_analysis.D: This is the quantity/time condition stated in §5.
choice_analysis.E: The special retail exception is not the Schedule II emergency prescription pathway.

related_facts: The question assumes the product already qualifies for the underlying §4 exception.
Section 5 then supplies the retail conditions.
explanation.mpje_trap: An exception from ordinary prescription control can still carry its own purchaser, quantity, and record requirements.

reasoning_steps: Accept the stem's premise that the product qualifies under §4
Apply the separate §5 retail conditions
Distinguish the pathway from ordinary prescription dispensing

questions.stem: A supplier receives a paper DEA Form 222 twenty days after execution. The form is otherwise timely, but the purchaser altered a Schedule II quantity after signing by writing over the original number. The purchaser asks the supplier to initial the change and ship the order. What is the best response?

choices.text: Fill the order because the form arrived within 60 days and timeliness cures execution defects.
Fill only the unaltered line items and correct the altered line after shipment.
Convert the altered paper form into a CSOS order by scanning it and adding an electronic signature.
Do not fill the defective form; the purchaser must issue a proper replacement order despite the original form still being within 60 days.
Wait until day 61 and then fill the form because expiration removes the need to address the alteration.

explanation.core_reasoning: A valid Form 222 must satisfy both execution/content rules and the time window. Here the form is timely but defective, so the supplier cannot use the 60-day rule to overlook the alteration.

choice_analysis.A: The 60-day validity period does not cure an altered or defective form.
choice_analysis.B: A supplier may not correct and fill a defective executed form in that manner.
choice_analysis.C: A paper Form 222 is not converted into a valid CSOS order by scanning it.
choice_analysis.D: Defect/execution validity is an independent gate from the 60-day time window.
choice_analysis.E: Expiration would create an additional reason not to fill the order, not cure the alteration.

related_facts: Form validity involves more than age.
A defective Form 222 cannot be corrected by the supplier and then filled as though properly executed.
explanation.mpje_trap: When two gates apply, passing the timing gate does not cure a separate execution defect.

reasoning_steps: Check the 60-day timing gate
Independently identify the altered form as defective
Apply the stricter defect consequence

questions.stem: A pharmacy mailed an executed paper DEA Form 222 to its supplier. The supplier reports that the form never arrived, no Schedule II goods were shipped, and the pharmacy cannot locate the original. The pharmacy still needs the order. What is the appropriate federal replacement process?

choices.text: Send the supplier a photocopy of the lost form and ask it to treat the photocopy as the original order.
Execute a new Form 222, attach the required statement identifying the lost form and nonreceipt of goods, retain the required copies, and make the applicable DEA loss report.
Ask the supplier to recreate the purchaser's lost form because only suppliers may issue replacement Form 222s.
Wait 60 days from the lost form's execution date; only after expiration may a replacement order be issued.
Treat the missing paper form as an inventory significant loss and file only DEA Form 106 without replacing the order.

explanation.core_reasoning: A lost executed Form 222 is handled through a replacement order plus a statement tying the replacement to the lost form and documenting nonreceipt. The registrant also follows the DEA reporting rule for lost or stolen order forms.

choice_analysis.A: A photocopy does not become the replacement executed Form 222 required after loss.
choice_analysis.B: This follows the replacement-statement and reporting framework for a lost Form 222.
choice_analysis.C: The purchaser executes the replacement order and required statement; the supplier does not recreate the purchaser's lost order form.
choice_analysis.D: The loss rule does not require waiting for the original form to age out before using the replacement procedure.
choice_analysis.E: A lost order form has its own Form 222 replacement/reporting procedure; it is not the same as loss of controlled-substance inventory.

related_facts: The replacement statement identifies the lost order form and the fact that goods were not received.
Loss of an order form and loss of drug inventory are different reportable events.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not reach for DEA Form 106 merely because the word 'loss' appears; identify what was lost.

reasoning_steps: Determine that the lost item is an executed order form, not drug inventory
Apply the replacement Form 222 and statement procedure
Apply the order-form loss reporting duty

questions.stem: A pharmacy's DEA registrant wants a staff pharmacist to sign paper DEA Forms 222 when the registrant is away. The staff pharmacist is not the person who signed the pharmacy's most recent DEA registration application. Which arrangement can lawfully provide signing authority?

choices.text: A verbal instruction from the pharmacy manager made before each order, with no retained authorization record.
A notation in the pharmacy's employee handbook stating that every licensed pharmacist may sign Form 222 automatically.
Use of the registrant's CSOS password to sign the paper form electronically.
A supplier's written permission authorizing the staff pharmacist to sign the purchaser's order forms.
A compliant power of attorney granted by the registrant and retained so it is available for inspection.

explanation.core_reasoning: Paper Form 222 signing authority can extend beyond the person who signed the DEA registration, but it must be conferred through the DEA power-of-attorney mechanism rather than job title, supplier consent, or shared credentials.

choice_analysis.A: Form 222 signing authority is not created by an undocumented verbal instruction.
choice_analysis.B: Licensure alone does not create the registrant-specific authority required to execute the order form.
choice_analysis.C: CSOS credentials do not substitute for the paper Form 222 power-of-attorney framework.
choice_analysis.D: The purchaser's registrant grants the authority; the supplier cannot confer it on the purchaser's employee.
choice_analysis.E: DEA permits a registrant to grant Form 222 execution authority through a compliant power of attorney.

related_facts: The power of attorney is retained for inspection rather than submitted with each order to DEA.
CSOS certificate authority and paper Form 222 power of attorney are related but distinct mechanisms.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not assume 'licensed pharmacist' automatically means 'authorized Form 222 signer'.

reasoning_steps: Identify who presently lacks direct registrant signing authority
Apply the DEA power-of-attorney pathway

questions.stem: A wholesaler receives an electronic CSOS order for oxycodone from a pharmacy. The order data are complete, but the wholesaler's validation system shows that the digital certificate used to sign the order was revoked before the order was transmitted. What should the supplier do?

choices.text: Ship the order because complete line-item data are enough even when the signing certificate is invalid.
Print the electronic order and treat the printout as a valid paper DEA Form 222.
Reject the electronic order rather than fill it on the revoked certificate; the purchaser must submit a valid authorized order.
Ship half the order because a partial shipment reduces the risk created by the revoked certificate.
Hold the order until 60 days after execution, when the certificate-revocation issue no longer matters.

explanation.core_reasoning: The supplier has its own CSOS validity gate. Complete product fields are not enough when the required DEA digital certificate is revoked or otherwise invalid.

choice_analysis.A: CSOS validity requires a valid DEA-issued digital certificate as well as complete order data.
choice_analysis.B: Printing does not convert an invalid CSOS signature into a valid paper order form.
choice_analysis.C: Supplier validation includes certificate validity, and a revoked certificate cannot support the required digital signature.
choice_analysis.D: Partial shipment does not cure an invalid electronic order.
choice_analysis.E: Time does not cure an invalid/revoked certificate; a valid order is required.

related_facts: CSOS relies on certificate validation and digital signature integrity.
A printout of an invalid electronic order is not a substitute paper Form 222.
explanation.mpje_trap: Electronic transmission is not synonymous with valid electronic authorization.

reasoning_steps: Check the electronic order data
Independently validate the signing certificate
Reject an order that fails the certificate gate

questions.stem: A pharmacy has already mailed a valid paper DEA Form 222 to its supplier for three Schedule II products. Before shipment, the pharmacy decides it no longer needs one line item but wants the other two. What is the appropriate federal way to stop that portion of the order?

choices.text: Send the supplier written cancellation of the identified line; the supplier documents the cancellation on the original Form 222.
Ask the supplier to erase the unwanted line from the executed original form before filling the remaining lines.
File DEA Form 106 for the unwanted line because canceling an order is treated as a significant loss.
Cancel the entire pharmacy DEA registration because a submitted Form 222 cannot be changed in part.
Wait for delivery, accept the unwanted Schedule II product, and destroy it because pre-shipment cancellation is prohibited.

explanation.core_reasoning: Once a paper Form 222 has been submitted, the purchaser does not alter the executed form. It sends written cancellation to the supplier, which documents the canceled item on the original form while processing any remaining valid items.

choice_analysis.A: DEA permits written cancellation of part or all of a submitted paper Form 222, with the supplier documenting it on the original.
choice_analysis.B: Erasure or alteration is not the lawful cancellation procedure for an executed Form 222.
choice_analysis.C: Cancellation of an unshipped order is not a theft or significant loss of controlled-substance inventory.
choice_analysis.D: DEA expressly provides a mechanism to cancel part or all of a submitted order.
choice_analysis.E: The purchaser may cancel before shipment using the written supplier-notification procedure.

related_facts: DEA permits partial or complete cancellation of a submitted paper Form 222.
Cancellation is different from a lost form, defective form, or inventory loss.
explanation.mpje_trap: Identify the transaction state: the form exists and is valid, but the purchaser wants to cancel part of an unshipped order.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the submitted Form 222 is otherwise valid
Identify that only part of the order is being canceled before shipment
Use written notice to the supplier
